content.rendered:
By Samuel L. Leiter

August 21, 2025: At last! The Delacorte Theatre, home of Free Shakespeare, in Central Park has reopened, after a two-year renovation costing a reported $85 million, with a production of one of Shakespeare’s most joyous and popular plays, Twelfth Night, or What You Will. But first, a word about this fabled outdoor theatre, which I have been attending since 1962, when it first opened. It was designed by Eldon Elder, my theatre design teacher at Brooklyn College, of whom we were all extremely proud. 

Elder’s essential design, happily, remains intact; aside from the attractive, new, redwood facing adorning the Delacorte’s exterior, the place looks much the same, the renovations being mainly to the infrastructure—seating, lighting, dressing rooms, elevator traps, and so forth, with—THANK GOD!—a do-over of the disgraceful adjacent bathroom facilities. These are shared with park users and will need careful supervision if they’re not to descend into filth again.

I wish I could be as upbeat about what’s on the stage. Twelfth Night, otherwise a perfect choice for reopening the theatre, filled as it is with love, laughter, and lyricism, has been staged by the estimable Saheem Ali, one of our most prolific and innovative directors, in what almost seems a desperate attempt to make sure the audience loves it. Such an approach, for this viewer anyway, results instead in the opposite.   

As in countless other Shakespeare in the Park revivals, the cast is studded with stars representing a diverse range of ethnicities and acting styles, mingling contemporary and traditional motifs, and incorporating abundant musical interludes. In a welcome bit of casting, Lupita Nyong’o plays Viola, while her real-life brother, Junior Nyong’o, plays her identical twin, Sebastian. The latter is a few inches taller, but, as mutually bewigged in dreadlocks by Krystal Balleza, they resemble one another much more closely than do most such Viola-Sebastian pairings.  

Peter Dinklage is Malvolio, Sandra Oh is Olivia, John Ellison Conlee is Toby Belch, Jesse Tyler Ferguson is Andrew Aguecheek, Daphne Ruben-Vega is Maria, Khris Davis is Orsino, b is Antonio, and Moses Sumney is Feste. The latter accompanies much of the action by singing his often indecipherable lines in a variety of familiar—if somewhat tuneless—pop styles (composer: Michael Thurber) while accompanying himself on an electric guitar.

Scenically, this Twelfth Night, designed by Maruti Evans, is among the sparest seen here, keeping the sizable expanse of the stage open except for huge letters running from one side to the other spelling the subtitle, WHAT YOU WILL. These are brilliantly lit by Bradley King to assume different colors as needed. When scenic units are required or need to be disposed of, they rise and fall via the elevator traps with which the stage is well equipped. The show assumes a playful attitude toward the text, in keeping with that ever-present subtitle, but this leads to an excess of theatrical shtick that often seems an excuse not to engage with the play’s characters as authentic people. 

Wearing modern dress stylishly enhanced with various fripperies by Oana Botez, the company cavorts with comic characterizations that rarely go beyond skin deep. Gimmicky choices abound. Orsino (Khris Davis) is a physically ripped, weight-lifting narcissist whose half-dozen well-suited courtiers are required to drop and do pushups if guilty of a faux pax. Sebastian and Antonio, shipwrecked, rise on a trap on a small, inflatable boat. The diminutive, Antonio— sexually ambiguous, with closely cropped hair dyed yellow—has the hots for his friend. Sebastian and Viola have a scene in Swahili. 

Andrew and Toby rise from beneath the stage in a hot tub, smoke dope and snort coke, and are joined by Maria. When Malvolio is secretly confounded by Andrew, Toby, Fabian, and Maria, the traditional bushes they hide behind are replaced with large letters spelling T-R-E-E held by the conspirators. The duel between Andrew and Viola is now a boxing match, with Andrew in boxer’s robe and shiny gold gloves. And, among the countless other such examples, the company enters for the crowd-pleasing, musical curtain call in a dazzling array of high-fashion, drag-style costumes. They must have cost a fortune, have nothing to do with the play, and would get them kicked out of Trump’s Kennedy Center if they ever showed up there.

This kind of broad, anything goes (i.e., what you will) elaboration of a famous play can work with a collaborative company joined by a common aesthetic built over time. In the present case, we have a bunch of actors creating something in a matter of weeks, and forced to adopt the first thing that comes to mind. This leads to cartoons rather than characters, and, while their natural appeal and intelligence help a few actors—like Sandra Oh, Lupita Nyong’o, and John Ellison Conlee—to swim, others, even such favorites as Daphne Ruben-Vega, Jesse Tyler Ferguson, and Peter Dinklage can’t help sinking.

Take Peter Dinklage, for example, as Malvolio, the role most male stars doing Twelfth Night would hunger to perform. It’s a role one can easily see him mastering, with his stentorian voice, serious demeanor, and sly intelligence. However, instead of Shakespeare’s self-righteous moralist disturbed by the childish antics of his nemeses, and driven by ambition, vanity, and desire for Olivia, we get a one-note, dour martinet, lacking nuance, and barely human. Dinklage mugs with clownish faces and quirky moves, the laughs coming mainly through the sight-gag of his stature. Malvolio, however, must be believably human so that, when he is treated brutally, he can earn our sympathy.  Dinklage is a popular and gifted actor and received applause on at least two exits, but his Malvolio feels more labored than inspired.

The same goes for this revival, which feels less like a coherent interpretation of Shakespeare’s comedy and more like a frantic, over-designed variety show that happens to use Twelfth Night’s plot as a loose framework. While the immense talent on stage is undeniable, it’s squandered in service of a concept that mistakes busyness for creativity and caricature for comedy. The renovation of the Delacorte is a magnificent gift to the public; it’s a shame that the long-awaited production chosen to reopen it misses the heart, poetry, and humanity of its chosen play.

Twelfth Night **
Delacorte Theater, Central Park at 81st Street, NYC.
Running time: 115 minutes with no intermission. publictheater.org
August 21 – September 14, 2025.
Photography: Joan Marcus

title.rendered: Jeff Ross: Take A Banana For The Ride ****

content.rendered:
By Samuel L. Leiter

August 18, 2025: In our currently niche-dominated entertainment world, including the infinitesimal number of choices on cable, streaming, and broadcast TV, it’s easy to be ignorant of many popular shows and artists, even if show biz is your biz. And thus was I ignorant of Jeff Ross, the 59-year-old stand-up comic who, apart from two onstage musicians (pianist Asher Denburg and violinist Felix Herbst), is doing a one-man gig at Broadway’s Nederlander Theatre.

When I saw his name in the show’s announcements, I figured this guy has got to be hiding his ethnicity behind that generic name, and sure enough, as he reveals early on, he’s really Jeffrey Ross Lifshultz. This, he explains, is “an old Hebrew word. It means you might want to change that,” which gets a big laugh. It’s the kind of joke Jackie Mason, whose real name was Yacov Moshe Maza, might have made. Ross, a paunchy fellow who enters through the audience in a banana-colored suit (smartly designed by Toni-Leslie James) with bits of glitter on it, obviously has Mason in his comic DNA. Also apparent are significant chunks of Don Rickles and Billy Crystal, to mention only the Jewish superstars that come immediately to mind.

While George Jessel was America’s “toastmaster general,” Ross (a name taken from his Grandma Rosie) is its “roastmaster general.” The audacious nature of the Rickles-like shtick that made Ross famous is available via YouTube, where I viewed his 2018 Comedy Central roast of pre-dementia Bruce Willis. On it, he not only mocks the Die Hard star but slings comments at Willis’s guests, poor Cybill Shepherd among them. As dumbfounded as she was when he asked if Elvis Presley had “gone down” on her, even that was not as outrageous as his comment at Jerry Stiller’s 1999 roast when the camera froze on Bea Arthur’s stunned face after Ross cracked, “Sandra Bernhardt, holy shit, I wouldn’t fuck you with Bea Arthur’s dick.”

That moment is recaptured in Ross’s new show during an early montage using video clips shown within the abundant arrangement of picture frames that compose the background of Beowulf Boritt’s attractively serviceable set, lit well by Adam Honoré. I don’t think Don Rickles would have gone quite so far, nor would Jackie Mason have used so much profanity, but it gives you a sense of where Ross’s sense of humor is often going.

In fact, though, while he slings some hilariously sizzling zingers, at audience members as well as people he references, and his language can be saltier than the Dead Sea, Ross’s 90-minute set actually leans more toward Billy Crystal-like sentimentality in its emphasis on his family history and beloved members. He embraces his Jackie Mason side when he launches into a routine near the beginning on how you shouldn’t mess with Jews, singing (if you could call it that) a funny, rhymed song warning people, “Don’t fuck with the Jews,” on which he gets the audience to join in. Some, I’m afraid, may feel uneasy warbling those lyrics if they begin to think about it.  

This comical defiance is related to the autobiographical framework in which he tells of growing up in Newark, NJ, where, like so many of his tribe, he learned how to fend off bullies by beating them with wisecracks. Family life—mom, dad, younger sister—centered around a successful catering hall, Clinton Manor, that his grandma created. It’s where he worked before a friend’s suggestion that he take a comedy class near New York’s Port Authority morphed into a successful career in stand-up.

There’s lots to enjoy and laugh at in his descriptions of his big-breasted mother, who died of leukemia when Ross was 14, and his fun-loving dad, who had a fatal encounter with coke when Ross was 19. The one-liners settle down for a while during some of the routine, and, while the show is a bit shy of mushy, it contains maudlin subjects that usually is able to transform into laughs. Poking fun at one’s physical ailments is an old trick I remember hearing from the Borscht Belt regulars Ross so obviously recalls. The completely hairless Ross manages to wring yocks not only from his alopecia areata, but from his colon cancer, which left him with a “semicolon,” and his, shall we say, two-eyed penis. 

And then there are his dogs. What can I tell you? His German shepherds, which he impersonates as heavily-accented Nazis, will steal your heart, not only from what he says, but from the video images we see. In fact, Ross’s entire life is abundantly visible on video clips, thanks to Stefana Bulbarella’s clever projection design, which adds immeasurably to both the laughter and the schmaltz. 

Ross avoids anything controversial, by which I mean politics, and is happy just making jokes about people’s personalities and looks. He celebrates other comics, especially deceased friends like Norm McDonald and Gilbert Gottfried, sings badly, and even does a dance step—if you can call it that—or two. For all the personal relationships he describes—especially a long segment on his late grandfather, whom he calls Pop Jack—he oddly skips the romantic side of life. Maybe I missed it, but the closest thing to billing and cooing I remember is his yowling with a canine. 

If you’re wondering about the show’s subtitle, “Take a Banana for the Ride,” it comes from Ross’s grandfather, who always advised him to do so when taking the bus into Manhattan. At the end, Ross and his crew distribute bananas in the audience, while additional personnel wait outside the theatre to give away even more. We can safely say, though, that, during its limited run, which ends on September 28, Jeff Ross will be killing it as Broadway’s top banana.

By Paulanne Simmons

August 16, 2025: Late in her life, Ava Gardner decided to write an autobiography. She didn’t so much want to tell her story as raise money. She was low on funds and as she famously said, “I either write the book or sell the jewels and I’m kinda sentimental about the jewels.” So she asked journalist Peter Evans to ghostwrite. 

All went sort of well until Gardner found out Evans had been sued by her former husband and sometime friend, Frank Sinatra, because he’d written about Sinatra’s association with the Mafia. Subsequently, Gardner worked with other ghostwriters to complete Ava: My Story, which was published  in 1990, shortly after her death. Evans, left with a lot of material, eventually wrote AVA: The Secret Conversations, published after both Gardner and Evans were dead.

Elizabeth McGovern (best known to British audiences as Cora Crawley, Countess of Grantham in Downton Abbey) thought Evan’s work would be a good source for drama because it concentrated mostly on the relationship between the actress and the writer. It also would give her an opportunity to show off her acting chops in the role of Ava. The play, directed by Moritz von Stuelpnagel, opened at the Geffen Playhouse in Los Angeles and is now at Manhattan’s City Center.

McGovern certainly had an interesting idea, but the problem is most people want to know about Gardner; few people really care about Evans. What makes the play even more lopsided is the acting. Aaron Costa Canis as Evans, creates a far more complicated and likable character than McGovern’s Ava, who seems to be bitchy, angry and vulgar throughout. 

What’s more, Canis opens and closes the show, has conversations with the offstage voice of his agent, Ed Victor (Chris Thorn) and easily morphs into the three men Gardner married: Mickey Rooney, Artie Shaw and most disastrously, Frank Sinatra. Canis even sings Cole Porter’s “I’ve Got You Under My Skin” in a more than decent imitation of Sinatra’s voice. He is indeed a talented actor.

While Evans wants all the dirt, Gardner wants to talk about her career. For the most part, Evans wins. The play tells us very little about the dozens of films Gardner acted in or the roles she played. On the other hand, we learn more than we need to know about her sex life, even though McGovern’s performance leaves us wondering exactly what made Ava Gardner so irresistible. 

Scenic designer David Meyer makes the play work better than he should with his Victorian boudoir that also allows for projections of the glamorous Gardner with her many lovers. But it is not enough to make us understand the tragic vulnerability of this flawed and passionate woman born in rural North Carolina and thrust unprepared into the intoxicating whirl of Hollywood at the tender age of 18.

CHARMING AND ENTERTAINING

By Alix Cohen

August 14, 2025: “Every story begins with a spark of imagination…” Jamie Allan was eight when his parents bought him a Fisher Price magic set. Dad was a fan of the art, built his son props (we’re shown one), and recorded famous magicians off the television. Between exposure and his first hands on experience, the boy lit up with aspiration. We see film of young Jamie. 

Onstage tonight is the original toy (with others of the period) ostensibly found while cleaning out an attic. “I spent the last 40 years of my life trying to recapture that feeling of wonder,” he says with gratitude. “The title of this show sets up expectation. It’s my job to inspire wonder.”

Fans of prestidigitation know that framing is paramount. Many practitioners present the same illusions, each hopefully with variation. The story holds one’s attention, bridging between effects, perhaps eliciting sympathy. Themed in the 1980s, Amaze takes us back to Allan’s formative years, what lead him to become a magician. It’s charming. He’s charming.

The Allans were musicians and pub owners. Jamie cut his teeth on performance in front of locals at The Horse and Jockey -shown in black and white graphic rendering. A feint with blank playing cards displays a unique way of identifying the one chosen by an audience member. Handheld video captures close-up work.

Jamie’s mom took him to an antique store (another nifty rendering) in search of a collapsible top hat for his burgeoning act.  Not only did the shop have one, but also tricks, props and books purchased from the estate of a magician. It was a treasure trove. (The Secrets of My Magic by David Devant, for example, can be found on eBay.) Mrs. Allan offered the boy successive items instead of pocket money. The haul was priceless.

Ten year-old volunteer Amalia mixes up jigsaw puzzle pieces. Jamie recollects his father hiding a piece from mom as puzzles took over their home. The girl chooses one. It turns out to be the only portion missing from another onstage puzzle. 

Every illusion relates to the performer’s childhood. (There are additional archival photos.) Specifics make history and tricks relatable. Spectacle he once longed to present is tendered by conjuring something weighty and sizable and levitating a woman who might’ve been his mom had she lived long enough. 

The latter proffers a unique and enchanting visual difference from the usual floating.  Both of these are staged almost with a shrug as if to say, ‘just something I threw on.’  The artist is genially Puckish.

Dad was really good with tech. The family had an early Betamax. Jamie and his father learned programming. One effect they created got the boy on BBC1. He became a professional before adolescence. Tonight the magician employs 4 digital screens creating artful, bewitching deception.

Getting back at an uncle that cheated his dad during a poker game required mastering a deck. Jamie demonstrates manipulation skill. His card hero was Cardini, much admired by master magician Ricky Jay as one of the all time greats of sleight of hand and stagecraft. Take notes if intrigued. There’s a clear path here.

The audience is involved in group participation gambits, several involving what seems like high math bent to Jamie’s will. Individuals, including some children, are called onstage to assist. There’s no pressure. He’s good with youngsters.

The well written show circles back time and again. A secret about the antique shop magic books is discovered years later. Something requested as audience initially sits takes center stage in an original reveal at the end. “You’re either a dreamer- you watch to enjoy, or a skeptic who approaches magic as a challenge,” Jamie Allan says. I, myself, am a dreamer. And you?

Directed by Jonathan Goodwin 
Illusion Manager- Justin Gentry 
Set Designer- Damien Stanton Sr.
Graphic Designer- Clare Nordbruch

By David Sheward

August 12, 2025: Bubba Weiler’s new play Well, I’ll Let You Go at the Space at Irondale in Brooklyn breaks a few rules and doesn’t seem to have much going for it at first. But the tension and emotion build gradually to a heartbreaking finish and the play dispenses many insightful observations about grief, family, and community along the way.

This is the playwright’s Off-Broadway debut and I’m only familiar with him as an actor. He gave a piercing performance in Swing State at the Minetta Lane in 2023 and was nominated for Drama Desk, Lortel and Outer Critics Circle awards. With this loving drama of everyday life, Weiler proves to be as thoughtful an author as he is a performer. 

The play opens without much theatricality. Scenic designer Frank J. Oliva’s environment is a mostly bare playing area with audience members on both sides. Avery Reed’s casual costumes are similarly understated, but they tell us much about the characters wearing them. There are a few pieces of simple furniture—a card table with two folding chairs, a group of six additional folding chairs arranged together, a mini-fridge, a table with a coffee maker and a microwave. The play begins with an actor entering without the house lights dimming. (They are not fully lowered until the final scene and the audience is so close they seem to be a part of the action. Stacey Derosier sparingly lights the play but her design achieves maximum impact.) Much like the Stage Manager in Our Town, the affable Michael Chernus explains the social and economy history of the setting and introduces the characters as they appear. This is a “get-by” kind of town of modest houses and strip malls where manufacturing jobs have disappeared to replaced by an Amazon fulfillment center. The house we’re in “attracts people who have had a rough go.”

We meet Maggie (a luminous Quincy Tyler Bernstine) and Wally (an endearingly nerdy Will Dagger), her husband’s needy cousin. The chattering, insecure Wally is complaining to Maggie about his mundane mail-carrier job, his paranoid fantasies that his boss and co-workers are out to frame him for an imagined crime, and annoying emails from travel companies urging him to take a vacation. Maggie lends a sympathetic ear as she feeds him leftover casserole. Simple enough stuff, written with attention to detail and played with verisimilitude. It’s slowly revealed Maggie has suffered a tragic loss. In succeeding scenes between Maggie and friends, strangers and family, we find out more (no spoilers). In each scene, the narrator relays the characters’ inner thoughts and backstory. This violates basic tenets of dramaturgy, having the subtext told to us rather than shown through indirect means. Nevertheless, the connection between the narrator figure and the central action becomes clear and his contributions are vital to the play. 

Each new character begins a new element into the story as well as props to fill out the setting. A forcefully jolly funeral director (quirky Constance Schulman) arrives with balloons. Maggie’s best friend and sister-in-law Julie (empathic Amelia Workman) brings on dozens of flower arrangements. Brother-in-law Jeff (Danny McCarthy, hiding guilt and shame behind bravado) accompanies a wheelbarrow full of mulch. Finally two women (equally devastating Emily Davis and Cricket Brown), previously unknown to Maggie, complete the puzzle and bring this sad but ultimately uplighting story full circle.

Throughout, Weiler’s dialogue and characterizations ring true, full of telling details. Each of the characters is fully realized both in the writing and the playing. Weiler paints a believable and touching portrait of a community in mourning, searching for answers to inexplicable violence. Jack Serio’s staging is simple and direct—there are no flashy confrontations or dramatic fireworks. This allows the understated performances of a sensitive cast to shine through. Every moment and detail tells us about the people. Even the dust on a neglected piano brought in for the last scene feels important.

Bernstine delivers an outstanding performance as the bereaved Maggie. You can read the history of her marriage, her life before that and her unfulfilled yearnings on her expressive face as Chernus relates this information (the smarter members of the audience will have figured out who he is early in the play). Chernus has the difficult task of standing outside the narrative, yet plays an essential role in it. He gradually moves from narrator to central figure and captures our hearts by the final moments.

Without revealing too much, Serio’s staging of the final scene is strikingly beautiful as Maggie’s world becomes more real and she receives comfort from an unexpected source. It reminded me of the memorable final act of David Cromer 2009 revival of Our Town when the universal became specific and we were all brought into the dead Emily’s painful memory of her 12th birthday. A similar feat of theatrical legerdemain occurs in the climax of this achingly moving work. The title tells it all—a seemingly off-hand remark that carries an emotional wallop.

By Isa Goldberg

August 11, 2025: Oddly, Bubba Weiler’s new play at the Irondale Brooklyn, Well, I’ll Let You Go, begins where the story ends …after Marv’s death. Being iconoclastic of structure renders a titillating edge to this dark comedy. In some cases, we better understand what has occurred when we see a later scene that brings out an earlier point in the story. 

As directed by Jack Serio, the play unfolds beautifully, like a Russian Doll constantly probed to reveal essence. And in the hands of an exacting cast – Michael Chernus (Severance), Quincy Tyler Bernstine (Tony nominee, Doubt), among others, it’s an intoxicating, intimate evening of theater that plays simply most of the time.

Performed on a three-quarter stage with the audience seated a few tiers above, it feels like peering into a fishbowl. Quite a beautiful one, with the natural wood floors of a big old country house, the openness of a family room, and the calm but penetrating light by designers Frank J. Oliva and Stacey Derosier respectively, create this world. 

So does the Narrator, Michael Chernus who tells us that Marv’s home is in a small Midwest town that has seen better days and so has its denizens. While on stage almost every moment of the play, the Narrator remains unseen and unnoticed by the characters performing the central action. But to the audience he is a calm and constant presence — listening to every word of the widow so intently that when he speaks, he is clearly responding to her as she sits on stage in a quandary about the loss of her husband. She can barely understand it. 

Now in her “Marvless life,” Maggie, in Bernstine’s understated portrayal, tries to untie the knot of loss. With remembrances of her deceased husband all around her, and visitors and phone calls from well-wishers needing to celebrate him as a hero, Maggie feels betrayed. That Marvin died to save a young woman’s life seems like more of a cover up – maybe there was a betrayal, she suspects.

Ironically Marv’s becoming a hero appears as unlikely to Maggie, as the troubled tribe of friends and family appear all too familiar, and predictable.  First, we meet Wally, who Marv always gifted with trays of food at Christmas because Wally couldn’t cook, and he couldn’t provide for himself. Will Dagger’s portrayal is just captivating, evoking a depth of empathy. 

Certainly, a lot more than the funeral director Joanie, who arrives with a treasure chest of funeral things – balloons, potpourri, breath mints. As played by the insanely comedic Constance Shulman, it looks like a multi-level marketing scheme. But as she digs deeper into her salespersonship, the Narrator reveals her motivation to us – to remain forever at her little boy’s funeral.

The funeral’s the thing around which the play evolves, and Maggie’s reluctance to have a funeral – to celebrate her heroic husband is the obstacle. And it builds to Maggie’s acceptance, her ability to say, “well, I’ll let you go.” As played by Bernstine it’s that ironic expression of self-realization in becoming a widow that we see in her face.  – “not Marvless like it is now, Marvless as if Marvless from the beginning. It almost feels good.”

While the story of loss, inexplicable loss mounts categorically, life moves on normally. If you haven’t hit rock bottom, you don’t live in this world. And if you do, it’s daily life, rife with coffee cups and banter.

But as the story builds conversation turns to a witch’s brew of negativity. Even Maggie’s dearest friend, played with perky neighborliness by Amelia Workman seems more like a medusa, threatening her with warnings about the need for a funeral to bring closure to the community.

Later Maggie will force her brother-in-law Jeff, played with raw sensibility by Danny McCarthy, to describe every detail of Marv’s death – the gunman at an abortion clinic, the young woman he was eyeing, and the community college to which he followed her. As Jeff describes him, the gunman was “a religious freak…he’s saying basically that maybe it’s time to — eye for an eye stuff, basically.”

When Maggie finally meets the mother of the young woman Marv saved – a high school student she had taught, she becomes able to fit the pieces together and achieve a sense of resolution about her husband. Visiting Maggie is less an act of guilt than honesty. In this role Emily Davis holds the underlying reality with vulnerability, and in a way that exposes the daily tragedies of people surviving poverty in small, isolated American towns.

Through this reveal, we finally meet Marv, a lawyer who served his community more than himself. As Maggie dresses him for his casket, they relive the bounty of their lives together. And so that the sanity and courage that Marv brought to this decaying world should never be lost. 

Indeed, an exemplary tale about one good man who changed the world around him and paid the price.

By David Sheward

August 7, 2025: “The story you are about to see is true…except for the parts that aren’t.” So reads a disclaimer flashed on the curtain before the start of Ava: The Secret Conversations, an intoxicating brew of Hollywood gossip and bedroom talk written by and starring Elizabeth McGovern as Ava Gardner, perhaps the most magnetic star to emerge from the studio system. We start from a point of unreliability but the veracity of information conveyed is not the point of the play, it’s capturing Gardner as she attempts to make sense of her chaotic life and earn enough money to pay her mortgage by publishing a memoir. 

McGovern is charismatic and stunning as the eccentric and glamorous Gardner. Clad by Toni-Leslie James in tasteful gowns and dresses subtly suggesting the pizzazz of old Hollywood, McGovern captures the ineffable “it” quality which made this woman a goddess on the screen. Simultaneously, she conveys her tender vulnerability as the star tries to analyze the impulsive choices which led her to being alone while being the most desired woman on the planet. She is raucously funny, punctuating nearly every sentence with the “f” word and then complaining “I hate foul-mouthed women!” Her Gardner is also frustratingly elusive as she dismisses the possibility of suffering abuse from the like of mysterious millionaire Howard Hughes. McGovern shows us all the facets of Gardner  from the wide-eyed North Carolina girl who rides to Tinseltown on the strength of a photograph in a Manhattan storefront to the cynical veteran of three marriages and numerous love affairs. “Love is nothing,” she spits out with venom, “it’s all a power play.” You can feel every twist and turn of a life’s roller-coaster ride in how McGovern delivers that line.

McGovern’s script is fast and fun and Moritz von Stuelpnagel’s staging flows brilliantly with the aide of David Meyer’s elegant, fluid scenery, Amith Chandrashaker’s subtle lighting and Alex Basco Koch’s cinematic projections which feature numerous clips of Gardner and her various husbands. At 80 intermissionless minutes, the author-star does not go very deeply into her subject’s motives and psychology. We get the greatest hits of Gardner’s dazzling life and career, much like the star’s own autobiography Ava: My Story.

The play is based on another Gardner tome, The Secret Conversations which consisted of taped talks between the star and writer Peter Evans who was contracted to co-author a book with her. Eventually, Gardner broke off the collaboration and published her own bio. Gardner put out the transcripts of their dialogues after her death.  

The action is seen from Evans’ point of view as he meets with Gardner in her London home and together they retrace her tumultuous life. In addition to playing Evans and masterfully narrating the action, Ganis does a credible job of impersonating the star’s three spouses—the hyperactive adolescent Mickey Rooney, the overbearing intellectual jazz musician Artie Shaw, and the blustering, rough-edged Frank Sinatra. Ganis is particularly impressive with his singing Sinatra. He sounded so much like the voice of America’s greatest pop male vocalist, I actually thought he might be lip-synching when he began to croon “I’ve Got You Under My Skin.” (Gardner’s love affairs with George C. Scott and bull-fighter Luis Miguel Dominguin are not included.)

Gardner calls Evans at odd hours, shamelessly flirts with him, pulls back when Sinatra expresses displeasure at her revealing their secrets, and finally pulls the plug. McGovern writes the breakup in metaphoric fashion with stagehands disassembling Meyer’s set and a director (Chris Thorn who also provides the voice of Evans’ agent) calling the shots for a final scene. McGovern enters as Gardner in a stunning red-carpet gown claiming “Someday everyone will get a chance to be famous” (a little too on the nose as a comparison to our social-media-saturated world) and disappears. Evans is finally left with projected images of the movie star and the sense he didn’t really get to know his subject at all. The audience might feel similarly short-changed. 

Ava: The Secret Conversations ***

content.rendered:
By Samuel L. Leiter

August 7, 2025: In 1988, former screen star Ava Gardner, famed much more for her sultry glamor (“the world’s most beautiful animal”) than her thespian artistry (although she did get an Oscar nomination), was living in London, recovering from a stroke and in need of money, when she asked British journalist-novelist-biographer Peter Evans (1933-2012) to ghostwrite her memoirs. A poor girl from a sharecropper family in Grabtown, NC, she’d gone to Hollywood in 1941, her striking beauty almost instantly leading to a movie career and a flamboyant sexual life. This included a yearlong marriage to diminutive MGM box office king Mickey Rooney when she was only 19 (and still a virgin) and band leader Artie Shaw, as well as, for two years, to crooner Frank Sinatra. Along the way there were entanglements with many other dashing figures, including Howard Hughes, Robert Mitchum, John Huston, famous bullfighters, and so on.

Initially hesitant—he was writing a novel—Evans soon realized the literary and lucrative possibilities in her juicy story and took on the assignment. His in-person and phone conversations with Gardner were dutifully recorded in pads and on microcassettes, eventually becoming a book, but not before Gardner fired him—he’d kept his relationship to Sinatra from her—and hired another writer. The new, less revealing book appeared in 1990, shortly after she died. Nearly 20 years later, in 2009, Evans decided to publish his account of working with the late actress; titled Ava: The Secret Conversations, it came out in 2013. Now, Elizabeth McGovern (“Downton Abbey”), another famous actress (if not on the same scale) has fashioned a play from it for her own performance. Having debuted at L.A.’s Geffen Playhouse, it’s now at City Center Stage 1. Given how much lively dialogue the book contains, it’s easy to see what drew McGovern to it.

McGovern, at 64, is a few years younger than Ava Gardner was in 1988. She remains an attractive, vivacious player whose notably slender figure complements her porcelain, girl-next-door prettiness. (She’s also more talented than Gardner.) Those, however, who may be expecting some physical approximation of the voluptuous movie star will not find it here, although McGovern wears an auburn wig (by Matthew Armentrout) resembling Gardner’s cropped coiffure as seen in a photo in the book. Even younger visitors unfamiliar with Gardner will notice this when her face and figure appear in the many brief clips (projections: Alex Basco Koch) projected on the upstage curtains of her living room, elegantly designed by David Meyer, and lit by Amith Chandrashakar. 

Nor will they hear Gardner in McGovern’s voice, which attempts to capture something of the film star’s sound and diction—drilled into her to erase her thick, rural, North Carolina accent—which never stays in one place long. McGovern understands Gardner’s impetuousness, her temper, her egotism, and her imperiousness; she also nails some of the comic lines with throwaway panache. But being entertaining doesn’t translate into being convincing, and therein lies the rub.

The Evans-Gardner memoir is unique, being as much about the writer’s efforts to corral the actress and get her to tell her story straightforwardly as it is about that story itself. The way it captures Evans’s thinking process as he struggles to keep Gardner focused, and to overcome her resistance to divulge material she feels uncomfortable about, makes it immensely readable. Gardner speaks in a colorful, earthy way, as freckled with profanity as any David Mamet play. She herself couldn’t believe how filthy her language was when she read Evans’s drafts. The conversations, by the way, on page and stage, are concentrated on Gardner’s personal relations and never grapple with her acting process or movie experiences, even when the subject arises.

While the majority of the play’s dialogue is lifted from the book, McGovern also provides lots of invention to fill out scenes that Evans doesn’t include, presumably gleaned from McGovern’s own research. But Gardner’s contributions, in which, despite her worrying about her memory, she recreates scenes with other people in detail, are always worth a listen. She reminds us that what she says may often be not what happened, only her version of it, but it usually carries the ring of truth. The play runs 90 intermission-less minutes; naturally, much about Gardner’s family and important Hollywood figures—John Huston, for example—she describes couldn’t be included. Fans of vintage Hollywood are advised to check out the original book.

McGovern, while physically off the mark, is costumed nicely by Toni-Leslie James, who gives her a touch more pizzazz—that red, silk dress!—than one might imagine from someone who usually wore a gray sweatsuit for her interviews. McGovern’s Gardner, by the way, seems little hindered by the effects of her recent stroke. And her smoking never resembles the way tobacco addicts like Gardner (who smoked even with emphysema) suck their ciggies.

McGovern has structured the play so that the same actor, Aaron Costa Ganis, plays each of her husbands, as well as Evans. There’s also the disembodied voice of book agent Ed Victor (Chris Thorn) heard over a loudspeaker when Evans needs to talk to someone else. Ganis tries very hard, but he’s far from being chameleonic, regardless of accent or tonal changes. Since he looks the same no matter whom he’s playing, the notion that he can somehow convince us he’s Mickey Rooney, Artie Shaw, or Frank Sinatra (whose singing he even imitates), much less the British-accented Evans, is doomed from the start. You may even be confused as to who’s who.

Worse, his Peter Evans ranges from fawning obsequiousness to whining neediness, never capturing the stealthy, subtle, chess master quality projected by the writer in the book. A times, he seems way out of his depth here. Although Evans grew fond of Gardner, her suspicions, mood shifts, tantrums, and changes of mind were a minefield he had to navigate with craft; his thinking out loud, where he offers his frustrations and strategies, is a principal feature of the book, where you come to appreciate how he handles his dilemma; in the play, he comes off as something of a boob.

The play—and Moritz von Stuelpnagel’s otherwise effective direction (including a scenic surprise near the end)—also makes his meetings with her more confrontational than they come across in the book. Ganis’s obviousness makes him lose the cat and mouse game of vigilant lion tamer trying to keep his wild animal not just from striking out but from devouring him.  

Before concluding, I must note that one of the book’s unforgettable topics is the size of Frank Sinatra’s penis, as vividly described by Gardner in Kitty Kelly’s book on the singer. Evans, told by Ed Victor he must confirm the verity of the account, finally gets the nerve to bring up the subject, and, in a highlight moment, gets a memorable response. The issue is mentioned in the play, but, inexplicably, there is no follow through. You might even call it a case of Chekhov’s gun, half-cocked.

By Samuel L. Leiter

August 7, 2025: In 1988, former screen star Ava Gardner, famed much more for her sultry glamor (“the world’s most beautiful animal”) than her thespian artistry (although she did get an Oscar nomination), was living in London, recovering from a stroke and in need of money, when she asked British journalist-novelist-biographer Peter Evans (1933-2012) to ghostwrite her memoirs. title.rendered: Joy: A New True Musical ** 1/2, Rolling Thunder ** 1/2

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

August 1, 2025: Joy, subtitled a New True Musical, Off-Broadway at the Laura Pels, is a serviceable enough product to entertain intermittently for two hours, but it’s basically a knock-off of stronger, more original female empowerment tuners such as Waitress, Wicked, Legally Blonde, and even Boop!, the recently departed cartoon fantasy. Based on the life of Joy Mangano, a struggling Long Island inventor who became a successful entrepreneur and media saleswoman through her Miracle Mop and other creations, Joy is fun and silly, but trods a familiar path lined with cliches. Note: Joy’s life also served as at the basis of a 2015 film starring Jennifer Lawrence.

Ken Davenport’s book is laden with stereotypes (chauvinistic execs, twangy Texans, fast-talkin’, flinty Long Islanders, 30-ish golddiggers matched with silver-chained daddies) and Annmarie Milazzo’s score heavily relies on generic tunes and unimaginative lyrics. But the game cast is professional and Lorin Latarro’s direction is brisk enough to hold our attention. There are occasional pops of wit and satire, but not to enough to push the show beyond just okay.

We start as beleaguered Joy (a commanding Betsy Wolfe) struggles to hold down her overflowing household. Not only is she putting up both her divorced, squabbling parents (Adam Grupper, Jill Abramovitz), but her ex-husband Tony (Brandon Espinoza) is bunking with Dad Rudy in the basement as Tony unsuccessfully tries to eke out a singing career. Joy’s mom Toots is permanently in her bathrobe and glued to the couch. Joy’s meager paycheck as an airline ticket clerk is the sole source of income, stressing her out and causing her to constantly miss soccer games and school events for her and Tony’s unhappy daughter Christie (Honor Blue Savage).

Joy has always had brights idea for gizmos which never panned out (realized in a musical number with a younger version of herself played by Nora Mae Dixon). Now she has a light bulb moment when she spills a glass of soda. Why not a mop that can wring itself out with the poor housewife user not having to bend over? Thus the Miracle Mop and a musical are born. 

There follows Joy’s against-the-odds sojourn to market her creation. She is pitted against  sexist QVC higher-ups (led by Charl Brown) and a Stetson-wearing villainous manufacturer named Cowboy Eddie (Paul Whitty) who attempts to purloin her patent. The former are given a rock alpha-male dance number complete with supposedly sexy hip thrusts, and the latter is joined by a chorus of central-casting cowboys (and a few token gals) in an intimidating hoedown. Choreographer Joshua Bergasse gives both numbers much needed energy.

Of course there is the obligatory, climactic power ballad in which the heroine defies the mostly male forces arrayed against her and received the obligatory sustained ovation. A parade of Joy’s subsequent products from coat hangers to luggage lines follows in the closing number. Ingenuity, woman power and capitalism triumph.

Betsy Wolfe vibrantly imbues Joy with spunk, splash and soaring vocals. She is the vital engine propelling the show, overcoming its weak points. The supporting company each gets a moment to shine, particularly Jill Abramovitz as Joy’s kvetching mother who ppwerfully puts over a moving song to express her mixed emotions of fear and pride about her daughter. Jaycee Macapuguy has moments of sassy fun as Rudy’s much younger girlfriend who invests in Joy’s mop. 

Tina McCartney’s costumes colorfully place in the late 90s era. Anna Louizos’ sets cleverly convey the chaos of Joy’s world with economy and style. I particularly enjoyed the shift from the living room to her Long Island environment. The home set flies out and a plethora of logos from Dunkin Donuts to Home Depot fly in. That’s a move Joy herself might have thought of. If only the show had more of that ingenuity and originality.

The rock revue Rolling Thunder at New World Stages is similarly uneven. Originally presented in Australia, this plotless evening employs hits from the 1960s along with excerpts from actual letters and interviews to provide nostalgic sentiment primarily and an understanding of that complex turbulent period secondarily. A cast of six talented actor-singers play composite characters who live through the US involvement in that tragic conflict. The fragmentary book by Bryce Hallett is basically an excuse to perform such anthems of the hippie generation as “Born to Be Wild,” “Gimme Shelter,” and “We Gotta Get Out of This Place,” with powerful arrangements and orchestrations by Chong Lim and Sonny Paladino. Director Kenneth Ferrone keeps the action moving, but not very imaginatively. Mike Tracey’s sound design emphasizes volume over clarity.

Wilson Chin’s nightmarish set mashes together Vietnam with America’s living rooms. Musicians are arrayed on platforms draped with camouflage nets while 1960s-era TV sets display programming from the era, ranging from Yogi Bear, The Jetsons, Star Trek, and The Carol Burnett Show to Walter Cronkite reading the news and footage of the war itself. 

The company does their best with the surface-level roles. Drew Becker, Justin Matthew Sargent and Daniel Yearwood feelingly play GIs enmeshed in the South Asian quagmire while Deon’te Goodman does the same for a protestor and other roles. Courtnee Carter gives depth and sensitivity to a nurse and an anti-war mother. Cassadee Pope conveys the broken heart and confused conscious of of one of the soldiers’ fiancee.

Jake DeGroot’s rock-concert lighting and Caite Hevner’s eclectic projection design provide variety of action which the book lacks.

By Paulanne Simmons

July 28, 2025: Gene Wilder and Gilda Radner were only married five years. Even though he was thirteen years older, she was married to SNL guitarist and bandleader G.E. Smith when she met Wilder and he had already been married twice, their marriage was a a happy one until she died of ovarian cancer at the age of forty-two. 

Cary Gitter’s Gene & Gilda imagines Gene Wilder telling the story of their courtship and marriage on a Dick Cavett interview. The play is often funny and sometimes poignant, but the lack of drama in Radner and Wilder’s relationship does not make for good theater. 

Jonathan Randell Silver is Wilder and Jordan Kai Burnett is Radner in Penguin Rep Theater’s off-Broadway premiere of Gene & Gilda at 59E59 Theaters. They are directed by Joe Brancato, who brings out much of the zaniness of their relationship, but never plunges into the depth of who these two talented and troubled people really are.

Silver and Burnett tell the story on Christian Fleming’s sterile white set. There are two large foam armchairs that are pushed around a lot and a door indicating that we are backstage at a recording studio. Overhead and behind them a grid of screens allows for video projections throughout. We hear Cavett’s voice, but we never see him.

At the beginning of the interview, Wilder insists on not talking about his wife’s recent death, but the ghost of Radner soon appears, forcing him to confront his loss. Burnett portrays Radner as smart, sassy and brutally honest. Wilder’s resolve crumbles when confronted with her “emotional blackmail.”

And so we see their on-again-off-again courtship, their continued success in their professional careers, Gilda’s futile attempts at becoming pregnant and her illness and death. Curiously, the best scenes of the play are when the couple dance together. As neither one of the comedic actors was known for dancing, this seems a strange choice. Yet these scenes works so well because they provide the few times we see Wilder and Radner actually doing something and not talking about what they have done.

Burnett is wacky and irrepressible. Silver is anxiety-ridden and reflective. It doesn’t seem like a match made in heaven, but somehow, we know from the beginning they will make it work. Gene & Gilda, however, doesn’t work as well as their marriage. For those who are true fans of the famous couple, the play may be a pleasant glimpse into their private lives. For others, it might be something of a disappointment.

By Alix Cohen

July 27, 2025: We live in an Instagram, TikTok driven society that makes successes of Influencers. Had Joy Mangano come up with her product a little later, she’d have used social media to sell. Celebrating imagination and tenacity as well as the little guy overcoming establishment is familiarly sympathetic –but a mop?! Well, you have to start somewhere. 

Joy (Betsy Wolfe, who looks very like Mangano), is sole breadwinner in a house of lazy dependents. Losing her job at TWA, she understandably panics. The house is mortgaged. No one’s trying very hard to bring in money. 

Divorced husband, Tony (Brandon Espinoza, milking cliché), a cocky vocalist/ musician, is so sure of his worth, he refuses back-up work. Also divorced, her retired Dad, Rudy (Adam Grupper, credibly hapless and sincere), is a dreamer and ladies’ man. He’s engaged to micro-mini-skirted Lorraine (well drawn Jaygee Macapugay), who went to high school with Joy. Tony and Rudy are prickly basement roommates.

Mom, Toots (Jill Abramovitz, think Eeyore in a housecoat), hasn’t been out of the house in two years. Soap operas are her world. Under the misguided pretense of being honest and protective, she criticizes the life out of her entrepreneurial child. Joy’s own smart daughter, Christie (deftly low key, Honor Blue Savage), has had it up to here with a mom who never shows up to her games.

Joy has contrived products since childhood. One of the more clever songs lists prototypes gathering dust. While mopping, she experiences a eureka moment. What will become the Miracle Mop wrings itself out. Its head can be removed to wash in a machine. A long handle allows one to stay upright while cleaning.“Do me a favor, spill something,” she instructs Christie. The original, homemade version is endearing.

The Manganos have no faith in Joy’s cockamamie ideas. When she arrives unannounced at QVC (Quality, Value, Convenience), the inventor faces a misogynistic review committee lead by Dan (a solid Charl Brown.) 

Suits protest the mop is too expensive and that women never buy from women. A production number declares We don’t just sell products, we sell stories! (appealing choreography by Joshua Bergasse) You’d think that would make the struggling, single mother a prime candidate.

How she gets on air and especially what ensues in front of the camera is a hoot. Success seems assured until it comes to light Rudy has made a foolish business deal with a snake oil representative named Cowboy Eddie (a terrific Paul Whitty.) Walking a tightrope above losing her patent and bankruptcy, Joy goes to court.

Betsy Wolfe has a powerhouse voice and adds emotional nuance to an otherwise unexceptional character. Her deer-in-headlights before QVC cameras is excruciating, impotent fury facing Cowboy Eddie palpable.

The book works well, characters and situations sufficiently drawn for a musical. Soft rock music and lyrics are pedestrian, arrangements good. Tony’s appeal to reconcile his family, Toots’s eventual embrace of Joy’s character, and particularly the heroine’s 11 o’clock number “A Better Way” lack specificity and skill. The show is cute, but overstuffed and wears thin. Its upbeat message, however, may bode successful touring.

Direction (Lorin Latarro) is crisp and buoyant with visual variety. Characters hold up. So much of the action is played to audience rather than to each other, however, veracity is diminished.

Sets (Anna Louizos) effectively slide in and out. Creativity comes to fore with the upgrade of home décor which includes an Andy Warhol-like silkscreen depicting four images of Joy, a Greek god garden statue, and a wall sculpture of metal leaves. Tina McCartney’s Costumes are era perfect, replete with double breasted suits and big-shouldered women.

An issue with Sound Design (Daniel Lundberg) finds lyrics buried in music/ unintelligible during many group songs.

Joy Mangano is a named inventor of 71 patent families and 126 distinct patent publications for her inventions

By Samuel L. Leiter 

July 25, 2025: The Vietnam war and the theatre have not exactly been strangers, although nowhere near as many shows, especially good ones, have taken their cue from it as they have from World Wars I and II. Not just straight plays, but Nam-based musicals have emerged from the conflict, which covered 1955-1975, with America involved from 1964. These shows have ranged from the humongous hit of Miss Saigon to lesser shows, like The Lieutenant, about the Mai Lai Massacre. 

All have used original scores, which opens the door for a musical based on the actual songs of the turbulent era, especially given the now iconic numbers that emerged in response to the political, social, and emotional turmoil the war stirred up. Stepping through that door at Off Broadway’s New World Stages is Rolling Thunder: A Rock Journey, a jukebox docu-musical, to coin a phrase, with a book by Bryce Hallett, based on a concept by Scott Barton, and 18 songs, most from the late 1960s. It’s not a bad idea, but the Rolling Thunder, well performed as it is, and even with great sound and lighting effects—by Jake DeGroot and Mike Tracey, respectively—creating the impression of a helicopter overhead, is no Miss Saigon.

Rolling Thunder, despite coming to us from Australia,tells the story of American involvement in the war—or at least it does now—by combining relevant, mostly still familiar songs of the era with a loose narrative following the lives of a small group of characters through their wartime experiences of the late 1960s. Four of the six actors (Drew Becker, Cassadee Pope, Justin Matthew Sargent, and Daniel Yearwood) play a single role throughout, while two (Courtnee Carter and Deon’te Goodman) play several each, although it’s not always clear who they are.  

There’s no plot per se, just the experiences and feelings of the characters as they live out the war. These are expressed, when they’re not singing, by commentary drawn from actual letters and documents of the period, with the actors delivering their lines directly to the audience; only a few moments bring two actors together for shared dialogue. Meanwhile, on a two-level concert-type stage designed by Wilson Chin sits or stands a band of five rock musicians, led by music director Sonny Paladino. Andrea Lauer has dressed everyone in a semblance of period garb, both mufti and military; one actor with prominent pectorals wears tops so tight you wish she’d given him a bra.

As the actors act or sing, or even demonstrate serious guitar chops, five upstage panels provide a nearly nonstop background of period video clips, designed by Caite Hevner, some with broadcast-type voiceovers, and several showing speeches from people like Lyndon Johnson or Walter Cronkite. Many images show the actual letters that the actors are speaking verbatim. Meanwhile, homefront antiwar protests compete with napalm bombings. 

On the stage proper is an assortment of multiple vintage TV sets, themselves showing 60s’ clips, including scenes from old TV shows. The show, directed at a high energy level by Kenneth Ferrone, is closer to a rock concert than to a book musical, and some of the numbers are choreographed like 60s-style Motown routines.

The letters cover the expected, even clichéd territory of soldiers going off to war filled with idealism and coming to grips with the hell of battle; love affairs with girls back home; parents’ concerns for their children and vice versa; the civil rights movement; physical trauma from combat, heat, and mosquitoes; loneliness; encounters with sex and drugs; postwar life, and so on. Their scattered presence as individual speeches, not dialogue, prevents us from deep concern with the characters, who usually speak to us rather than each other even when two of them are in a scene together. Dramatically, if not thematically, this showis more of a sun shower than a thunderstorm.

Audiences will, of course, be mainly concerned not with these cardboard characters or the history lessons this defiantly antiwar show frequently wishes to convey (one section bombards us with facts and figures about casualties). Fans of the period’s music will instantly recognize songs like the Stones’ “Gimme Shelter”; Kris Kristofferson’s “Help Me Make It Through the Night”; “War,” popularized by Edwin Starr; the Animals’ “House of the Rising Sun” and “We Gotta Get Out of This Place”; Steppenwolf’s “Born to Be Wild”; Barry McGuire’s “Eve of Destruction”; Bob Dylan’s “A Hard Rain’s A Gonna Fall”; “Killing Me Softly,” a bit anachronistic here, since Roberta Flack’s cover didn’t arrive until 1973; and “Bridge Over Troubled Waters,” by Simon and Garfunkel, and so on.

One can easily compile a list of other pertinent Vietnam-era songs that might have been chosen, but perhaps there were rights problems with numbers like “I-Feel-Like-I’m-Fixing to Die Rag,” by Country Joe and the Fish; “Chain of Fools,” by Aretha Franklin; “Proud Mary,” by Creedence Clearwater Revival; “Give Peace a Chance,” by John Lennon, and many others.

Although the songs in Rolling Thunder are worked into the script at junctures to which their tone and lyrics have some relevance, they are performed, for the most part, not to suggest their significance in a character’s life, but, with a cast of one power voice after another, as one-offs squeezing each song for as much of its musical and lyrical power as possible. Even “Bridge Over Trouble Waters,” the finale, gets the all-stops-out treatment. The succession of overly amplified songs, with an excess of the inflated shouting and musical histrionics we expect at a rock concert, becomes monotonous; it’s also probably downright dangerous to sensitive eardrums.

Rolling Thunder rocks for two hours; I was ready to roll after an hour and a half. 

Rolling Thunder **1/2

By Paulanne Simmons

July 24, 2025: Rolling Thunder was the name of a Bob Dylan concert tour that also featured performers such as Joan Baez, Joni Mitchell and Ramblin’ Jack Elliott. And it was the title of the film Martin Scorsese made about the tour. Rolling Thunder is also an advocacy group for Vietnam  POWs and MIAs, whose annual event is a slow motorcycle ride in Washington, D.C. on Memorial Day. Now it is a rock journey about the Vietnam War that comes from Australia and is making its New York premiere at New World Stages.

Rolling Thunder is a play, a documentary and a concert. Bryce Hallett has written a series of searing monologues for Rolling Thunder, that explores the war from the point of view of the soldiers who fought it and their girlfriends and parents, who  stayed home waiting for their return.

The stellar ensemble cast (Drew Becker, Deon’te Goodman, Justin Mathew Sargeant, Daniel Yearwood and Ethan Hardy Benson are the soldiers, Cassadee Pope and Erin Ramirez are the girlfriends and  Courtnee Carter is the mother), directed by Kenneth Ferrone, portrays soldiers who were drafted and soldiers who enlisted, a girlfriend who remains faithful and a girlfriend who writes a Dear John letter.

Much of Hallett’s dialogue is poetic. It is always moving. The soldiers describe their terror and their despair, their love and respect for their comrades, and sometimes for the Vietnamese. 

The monologues alternate with songs that were both popular during that era and like a Greek chorus, provide commentary and context for what is happening onstage. Thus we hear songs like “Eve of Destruction,” “The Letter,” and “We Gotta Get Out of This Place” at just the right times.

Chong Lim & Sonny Paladino’s arrangements and orchestrations are both original and true to the most popular versions we know so well. “Killing Me Softly with His Song” and “Help Me Make It Through the Night” are heartbreakingly rendered. “A Hard Rain’s A-Gonna Fall” and “All Along the Watchtower” are as ominous as Bob Dylan intended. And “Bridge Over Troubled Waters” spreads the gospel of love.

Videos, such as one of President Nixon explaining why he is going to pursue the war and Walter Cronkite commenting that the war can only end in stalemate, give the individual stories wider significance and add verisimilitude. 

The show ends with statistics about the wars casualties projected on screens behind the actors and musicians, and a video of the names on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C. At a time when only volunteers fight and die for our country it is often too easy for average citizens to distance themselves from the casualties. Rolling Tunder makes abundantly clear who these men and women are and what they are called upon to sacrifice.

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

July 24, 2025: The Glimmerglass Festival in Cooperstown, NY celebrates its 50th anniversary season with departures from traditional operatic fare. In addition to Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s Sunday in the Park with George, an unconventional Broadway musical in both its form and content (previously reviewed), the Festival is presenting The House on Mango Street, a world premiere opera based on Sandra Cisneros’ beloved coming-of-age novel featuring an eclectic score by Derek Bermel, and Igor Stravinsky’s 1951 The Rake’s Progress which employs 18th century forms through a modernist lens. The results of these stylistic blendings are bracingly exciting in both productions.

It’s hard to imagine Mango Street in stage or operative form since the original is a kaleidoscopic series of short vignettes detailing the adolescence of Esperanza, a Latina teen growing up in an immigrant neighborhood in Chicago. The libretto by Cisneros and Bermel fashions the fragments of the novel into a dazzling, cohesive tapestry. Just as the libretto stitches together the myriad threads of Esperanza’s story and her numerous friends, relatives, and neighbors, Bermel’s score incorporates many different musical styles to reflect the diverse milieu of the plot. No less than 13 different genres can be detected, ranging from salsa, ranchera, mariachi, and Tex-Mex to rap and hip-hop with touches of gospel, polka, and klezmer. Somehow these disparate elements come together to form a harmonious whole, under conductor Nicole Paiement’s baton, just as the bits and pieces of Cisneros’ novel do. 

Chia Patino’s direction manages to keep the multiple storylines clear with the aide of John Conklin’s suggestive sets, Amith Chandrashaker’s versatile lighting and Greg Emetaz’s evocative projections.

Before the first note of music is played, the audience can hear a strange metallic sound. When the curtain rises, we see that noise is being made by Esperanza (expressive Mikaela Bennett) typing on an old-fashion manual model at what appears to be a kitchen table. Behind here is a scrim upon which dozens of sentences from Cisneros’ novel are projected. From here we are taken into Esperanza’s world as Conklin’s set consisting of two large, wooden-frame houses are rolled on stage. We meet the various characters of the neighborhood as her family moves in. There’s eccentric Cathy, Queen of Cats (delightfully daffy Catherine Thornsley costumed by Erik Teague in imaginative, feline-festooned finery); siblings Lucy and Rachel (funny Samantha Sosa and Kaylan Hernandez) who promise to be Esperanza’s friends forever if she will give them five dollars to buy a bike; Sally (outstanding Taylor-Alexis DuPont), the sassy local flirt who covers up the abuse she suffers at home with a boisterous presence; and cynical landlady Edna (marvelously dry Tzytle Steinman) and her sister Ruthie (magnificently melancholy Natalie Corrigan) who longs for her romanticized past and bemoans her disappointing presence. 

Drifting on the edges of the action is Geraldo (heart-thugging Angelo Silva), a food-cart vendor and undocumented immigrant who is tragically shot during a block party. When the police come to investigate, no one can provide his last name or any info about him leading to a wrenching group number on the plight of the undocumented, led by Alicia (bold Sarah Rosales), a college student also dealing with immigration issues. This theme is made even more relevant by the cruel policies of the current Trump administration. 

The main thread running through the multiple story arcs is Esperanza’s yearning to  escape her neighborhood for the grownup world outside. She reaches a catharsis after being assaulted by two neighborhood boys and is healed by three shaman women in a metaphysical, metaphorical ritual, stunningly staged by Patino. Throughout Mikaela Bennett delivers a complex, compassionate portrait of the conflicted Esperanza both dramatically and vocally in this marvelous House on Mango Street.

Igor Stravinsky’s The Rake’s Progress also fuses varying styles and timelines. Premeiring in 1951 in Venice, Rake’s eloquent, poetic libretto by W.H. Auden and Chester Kallman is loosely based on a series of 18th century paintings and engravings by Hogarth depicting the downfall of the morally untidy Tom Rakewell as he succumbs to the temptations of money and the flesh. Stravinsky’s score is a melding of dissonant modernism and classical forms, brought to vivid life by conductor Joseph Colaneri. Director-choreographer Eric Sean Fogel has converted the setting to the time of the composition (Lynly A. Saunders designed the sleek period costumes). Fogel’s fluid, Fosse-like staging keeps the action moving (several of the brothel scenes resemble Fosse’s grope-y groupings in Sweet Charity) and the splendid cast displays impressive vocal chops and acting skills. 

Adrian Kramer is a robust, muscular Tom, running the gamut from arrogant self-satisfaction when Tom is on top of the world to desperate desire when he lands in Bedlam asylum believing he is the lovelorn mythological figure Adonis. Lydia Grindatto has a clear, floating soprano as Anne Truelove, Tom’s long-suffering betrothed. Aleksey Bogdanov is a deliciously charming, but ultimately devious devil figure as Nick Shadow, with a devastating bass-baritone. Deborah Nansteel brings panache, flair, and humanity to the usually comic role of Baba the Turk, a bearded lady whom Tom marries for kicks. Marc Webster provides sturdy support as Anne’s father. This is a refreshing new take on one of the most challenging pieces in the modern operatic canon.

The abstract set by John Conklin is transformed into a nightmarish hells cape by Robert Wierzel’s red-tinged lighting and Greg Emetaz’s mod projections.

The House On Mango Street ****

title.rendered: The Gospel at Colonus ****, Sunday in the Park with George ****

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

July 21, 2025: Musical styles are mixed to maximum emotional effect in unusual productions in one new outdoor venue in Manhattan and at the 50th anniversary season of a long-established festival in upstate New York. Lee Breur and Bob Telson’s The Gospel at Colonus returns in a soul-stirring staging in the Amp at Little Island, affording spectacular views of the Hudson River as a galvanizing cast retells the Oedipus myth with passion and fervor. Meanwhile in Cooperstown, New York, the Glimmerglass Festival celebrates its golden anniversary with a moving world premiere (The House on Mango Street) and a pair of innovative, imaginative restagings of two modernist classics from Broadway and the opera repertory (Sunday in the Park with George, The Rake’s Progress).  

The Gospel at Colonus has an unusual production history. After opening at the Brooklyn Academy of Music in 1983 and winning an Obie Award, the adaption of Sophocles’ tragedy Oedipus at Colonus set in an African-American Pentecostal church service was performed to acclaim in Washington, DC, Philadelphia and Atlanta and was filmed for PBS. An unlikely Broadway transfer in 1988 starring Morgan Freeman ran for only 61 performances and received only one Tony nomination (for Breuer’s book). 

Breur’s original production was on a grand scale with an enormous choir. Shayok Misha Chowdhury’s new staging is more intimate with David Zinn’s minimal set suggesting sylvan glades and ancient ritual environments. The role of Oedipus, seeking sanctuary and shelter just before his death after a tragedy-strewn reign as king of Thebes, was originally taken by the Five Blind Boys of Alabama. (This casting echoed Oedipus’ horrific self-blinding after discovering he had unknowingly killed his father and slept with his mother.) Here his lines and solos are divided between an intense Stephanie Berry who also serves as narrator and preacher of the service, and operatic bass-baritone Davone Tines and jazz singer Frank Senior. 

The theme of Breur’s adaptation is redemption and salvation after suffering, drawing parallels between Christian theology of love and forgiveness and the Greek emphasis on man’s inevitable fall from grace through hubris. All three Oedipus figures deliver heart-breaking performances, each of their individual styles blending into a harmonious whole. Spectacular vocal variety is on display by Samantha Howard and Ayanaa George Jackson as Antigone and Ismeme, Oedipus’ grief-stricken daughters, Kim Burrell as the noble Theseus, Jon-Michael Reese as Oedipus’ craven son Polyneices, and Brandon Michael Nase as the Balladeer. Dr. Kevin Bond is a frightening figure as the villainous usurper Creon. Bob Telson’s rollicking, emotional score is given ample metaphorical blood, and literal sweat and tears (and invoking the same from the audience) by the glorious cast and chorus, thanks to co-music directors Dionne McClain-Freeney and James Hall. 

Like Gospel, Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s Sunday in the Park with George did not receive universal acclaim when it opened on Broadway in 1984. Sondheim’s eclectic and innovative score and Lapine’s thought-provoking book and direction were greeted with cautiously mixed reviews and the Tonys for Best Musical, Book and Score went to Jerry Herman and Harvey Fierstein’s more stylistically conventional La Cage Aux Folles (though its depiction of a loving gay male couple was revolutionary for tis time.) Sunday subsequently won the Pulitzer Prize, had a decent run of 604 performances, two well-received Broadway revivals, and has achieved status as a jewel in the Sondheim and musical theater crown-canon.  

The Glimmerglass Festival continues its bold programming choices by presenting this unusual musical along with operatic fare. The story is a fictionalized account of the groundbreaking impressionist painter Georges Seurat and his massive pointillist masterpiece A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte. In the first act, we witness the creation of the painting and the breakup of Georges’ relationship with his model and lover, Dot. The second act leaps ahead 100 years and Georges’ great-grandson, another artist also named George, is facing a similar crisis in finding his creative identity. The sojourn of both Georges echoes Sondheim’s seeking new musical paths and encountering short-sighted criticism (The song “No Life” in which Jules, a fellow painter, and his wife Yvonne carp about Seurat’s seemingly cold approach, could be about modern reviewers complaining about Sondheim’s lack of traditional melody.) 

Ethan Heard’s direction skillfully balances the author’s observations on art and the creative temperament with emotional veracity. He has the company act as a sort of Greek chorus, sitting at the sides of set designer’s John Conklin’s bare raised platform, physically expressing the raging dispute between Georges and Dot (Madison Hurtle is movement director.) In the beautifully staged climax of Act One where Georges uses the actors to create the famous painting, Heard adds a sensitive staging detail. He has Georges bring Dot her hat as seen in the painting and place it lovingly on her head, recalling the earlier song, “Finishing the Hat,” an anthem to artistic drive and the necessary personal compromises a great artist must make. In the second act, Heard makes clever use of the advanced technology of Greg Emetaz’s projection design during “Putting It Together” with silhouettes of George frantically popping all over the set, even on a waitress’ serving tray, as the frazzled creator flits from potential patron to critic to fellow toilers in the arts fields. Amith Chandrashaker’s painterly lighting and Beth Goldberg’s century-spanning costumes adds variety and punch.

As both Georges, John Riddle’s shimmering tenor captures the conflict between creativity and personal connection. Marina Pires feelingly conveys Dot’s desperate hearing to be loved and to understand her artist-lover and is dry and funny as Dot’s daughter Marie, an elderly sage in the second act. Marc Webster and Claire McCahan make for a properly pompous Jules and Yvonne. Loretta Bybee is sharp and witty as Georges’ mother and a contemporary arts writer. Conductor Michael Ellis Ingram provides a lustrous rendition of Sondheim’s sumptuous score, combining Broadway brash with modernist modes.

Reviews of Glimmerglass’s The House on Mango Street and The Rake’s Progress will follow.

The Gospel at Colonus ****

title.rendered: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance ****

content.rendered:
By Paulanne Simmons

July 16, 2025: It has been said, with a good deal of truth, that short stories make the best screenplays. This is certainly the case with the film, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, based on a short story by Dorothy M. Johnson. But Jethro Compton’s play shows short stories can also be successfully adapted for the stage. It is definitely a pleasure to see how Onomatopoeia Theatre Company, on a limited budget and in a small theater, has created such an intense and engaging production.

First of all, kudos go to director Thomas R. Gordon for putting together an excellent cast and directing with such verve. And Nino Amari has created a single unit set, with bar, piano and table and chairs, that efficiently recreates what we have come to imagine a saloon to be. But most important, it is the excellent acting which makes this play so much more than a simple good guys versus bad guys western.

Leighton Samuels is Ransome Foster, a loner from New York who has studied law and reads books. He is delivered to Hallie Jackson’s Prairie Belle Saloon by cowboy  Bert Barricune (Samuel Shurtleff), who found him bruised and battered after a run-in with the local outlaw, the infamous Liberty Valance (Derek Jack Chariton). 

Ransome is nursed back to consciousness by Hallie (Mari Blake), Bert and “The Reverend” Mosten (Daniel Kornegay), the cook, who helps Hallie run the place and keeps her on the right track in life. His position as a Black man in a small western town during a time of sweeping racism is precarious.

 If fireworks do not immediately ensue between Hallie and Ransome, it’s obvious they will eventually be drawn to each other. But The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance is not so much a love story as a tale of valor. Foster must eventually show his grit when Valance comes to wreak vengeance on him for his attempts to civilize the frontier. Valance knows the educated population will not tolerate his lawlessness. Ransome knows he cannot give in to the forces of evil.

Blake has a nice take on the tough girl with a good heart theme. And Samuels is an effective good guy, even if his accent sounds more Jewish than New York. His valor is carefully balanced with the hesitation and incompetence of someone who knows he might have taken on more than he can handle. But Chariton takes over the stage with his bitter sarcasm and ruthless energy. Together Samuels and Chariton create the kind of explosive interactions that make theater such a powerful experience.

Much like that other famous western, High Noon, this is a morality tale, pitting good against evil, courage against swagger and civilization against chaos. The lesson is one we must learn again and again.

The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance ****
